prompt.context: Our client, GoNet, is a US-based Internet Service Provider (ISP) that is considering entering the European market. They are currently the dominant player in the US with two revenue streams: a subscription access fee and by taking a percentage of all e-commerce transactions from subscribers. Examining the European market, GoNet has found that the market is highly fragmented and ripe for entry.
prompt.question: You are going into a meeting with the CEO and have been asked to perform some quick 'back of the envelope' calculations to determine the potential profitability of entering Europe.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape in Europe?
clarifying_info.a: The industry is highly fragmented. No information about market leaders or trends.

clarifying_info.q: How many subscribers does GoNet plan to capture in Europe?
clarifying_info.a: GoNet plans to capture a base of 10 million subscribers.

clarifying_info.q: What will the subscription fee be?
How much do subscribers spend online and what commission does GoNet take?
clarifying_info.a: The average GoNet subscriber purchases $1,800 of goods on the internet annually; GoNet receives a 3% commission.
Fixed costs are $1 billion annually; variable costs are $110 per subscriber annually.

exhibits.title: Math Information (Part 1)
exhibits.shows: A summary of key assumptions for the quantitative analysis: subscriber count, monthly subscription fee, annual online spending per subscriber, commission rate, fixed costs, and variable cost per subscriber.
exhibits.data: 10 million subscribers; $20/month subscription fee; $1,800/year of online spending @ 3% commission; Fixed costs: $1 billion; Variable cost: $110/year per subscriber

exhibits.title: Math Information (Part 2)
exhibits.shows: Continuation of the quantitative scenario with the same base assumptions, used for breakeven and subscriber count calculations.
exhibits.data: Same base assumptions as Exhibit 1, applied to questions about required online spending per subscriber to maintain profit levels and the minimum subscriber count to break even

framework: Revenue analysis: Calculate two revenue streams — subscription fees and e-commerce commissions — under current and stress-test assumptions
Cost analysis: Separate fixed costs ($1B annually) from variable costs ($110/subscriber/year) to determine total cost structure
Profitability calculation: Derive annual net income and gross margin under baseline assumptions
Sensitivity / stress testing: Evaluate impact of price pressure (competitor entering at $10/month) on profitability
Break-even analysis: Determine minimum required subscriber spending and subscriber count to reach break-even under price-compressed scenario
Qualitative assessment: Address cost reduction options, strategic rationale despite losses, key risks and benefits, and final recommendation

questions.prompt: 1) Please determine the annual net income (before taxes) in Europe, given the current revenue model and set of assumptions. What is the annual gross mark-up, in percentage?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate subscription revenue (10M x $20 x 12) and commission revenue (10M x $1,800 x 3%), then subtract total fixed and variable costs. Strong answers identify both revenue streams clearly and compute margin.

math.setup: Subscription revenue = 10M subscribers x $20/month x 12 months. Commission revenue = 10M subscribers x $1,800/year x 3%. Total costs = Fixed $1B + Variable (10M x $110).

questions.prompt: 2) GoNet just found out that a new entrant is charging $10/month and capturing market share. Can we lower our fee to $10/month?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recalculate subscription revenue at $10/month, keep commissions constant, and compare to total costs. Should conclude the answer is No and ideally discuss demand elasticity.

math.setup: New subscription revenue = 10M subscribers x $10/month x 12 months. Commission revenue unchanged at $540M. Total costs remain $2.1B.
math.answer: No — cutting to $10/month results in a $360M annual loss. The market is highly elastic, meaning GoNet cannot win enough subscribers at $20/month, but cannot profitably operate at $10/month without other changes.

questions.prompt: 3) With high market elasticity, GoNet will not be able to charge more than $10/month. How much would each subscriber have to buy on the Internet to keep profits at the same level as the $20/month scenario?
questions.guidance: Candidate must work backwards from target profit ($840M) to determine required commission revenue, then convert to per-subscriber spending. Should flag that the result is unrealistic.

math.setup: Target net income = $840M. Total costs = $2.1B, so total revenue needed = $2.94B. Subscription revenue at $10/month = $1.2B. Required commission = $2.94B - $1.2B = $1.74B. Per subscriber commission = $1.74B / 10M = $174/year. Required annual spending per subscriber = $174 / 3%.
steps: Required annual online spending per subscriber = $174 / 0.03 = $5,800/year
math.answer: Each subscriber would need to spend $5,800/year online — more than 3x the current $1,800 baseline. This is unrealistic.

questions.prompt: 4) How much would each subscriber have to buy on the Internet to enable GoNet to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate must find the minimum commission revenue to offset costs when subscription revenue is $1.2B. Should note this is still unrealistic (>50% increase from current spending).

math.setup: Break-even: total revenue = total costs = $2.1B. Subscription revenue = $1.2B. Required commission = $2.1B - $1.2B = $900M. Per subscriber commission = $900M / 10M = $90/year. Required annual spending = $90 / 3%.
math.answer: Each subscriber would need to spend $3,000/year online — a >50% increase from the $1,800 baseline. Also unrealistic.

questions.prompt: 5) Given that we cannot charge more or realistically increase shopping significantly, how many subscribers would we need in order to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate must compute incremental profit per subscriber then divide fixed costs. Must remember to subtract variable costs from per-subscriber revenue. A common mistake is forgetting variable costs.

math.setup: Revenue per subscriber at $10/month: ($10 x 12) + ($1,800 x 3%) = $120 + $54 = $174/year. Variable cost per subscriber = $110/year. Contribution margin per subscriber = $174 - $110 = $64/year. Break-even subscribers = Fixed costs / Contribution margin per subscriber.
math.answer: GoNet would need approximately 15.625 million subscribers to break even — 56% more than the assumed 10 million base.

brainstorming.prompt: How could GoNet reduce the fixed costs of investment? Would there be any reason to continue with the investment even if it will lose money? What other risks or benefits should GoNet consider?

categories.name: Fixed cost reduction levers
ideas: Outsource network capacity to third-party providers
Lease existing network infrastructure rather than building
Focus on specific geographies or cities rather than pan-European rollout
Partner with local ISPs to share infrastructure costs

categories.name: Strategic reasons to proceed despite losses
ideas: Establish a foothold in European internet retailing
Expand subscriber base as a long-term investment
Use entry as a loss leader to build brand and scale
Option value: learn the market before competitors entrench

categories.name: Additional risks
ideas: Regulatory and compliance differences across EU countries
Currency risk (USD/EUR) affecting cost and revenue
Incumbent ISPs reacting aggressively to new entrant
Inability to reach 15.6M subscriber break-even threshold
Technology infrastructure gaps in some European markets

categories.name: Additional benefits
ideas: Access to growing European e-commerce market
Network effects if subscriber base scales rapidly
Cross-selling US business relationships to European subscribers

recommendation: Based on initial estimates at $20/month, the European market appears attractive with $840M annual net income and a ~29% margin.
However, given high market elasticity and a competitor at $10/month, the economics deteriorate sharply — GoNet would lose $360M annually at $10/month with only 10M subscribers.
To break even at $10/month, GoNet would need 15.6M subscribers (56% above plan) or subscribers spending $3,000/year online (67% above baseline), both of which appear unrealistic in the near term.
Therefore, entry is not recommended under current assumptions without a differentiated strategy.
risks: Price compression from fragmented, elastic market
Inability to achieve the 15.6M subscriber count needed to break even
Overestimation of European e-commerce spending per subscriber
High fixed cost base with limited ability to reduce quickly
next_steps: Conduct market research to validate elasticity assumptions and realistic subscriber acquisition targets
Explore cost reduction strategies: outsourcing, leasing, geographic focus
Investigate whether a differentiated product (e.g., premium features, exclusive content) could support a price premium above $10/month
Model scenarios with a tiered pricing structure to capture both price-sensitive and high-value segments
